info.name: Jackpot Contribution and Reward Service
info.description:
Every endpoint of the jackpot service, plus a runnable walkthrough that wins a jackpot end to end.

**Before you start**

1. Run the service: `docker compose up -d --build`, or `mvn spring-boot:run -Dspring-boot.run.profiles=no-kafka` for the broker-less mode.
2. The `baseUrl` collection variable defaults to `http://localhost:8080` — override it in an environment if needed.

**The walkthrough folder** is ordered and stateful: run it with the Collection Runner (folder → Run). It publishes a bet, waits for the Kafka consumer to contribute it, pushes the demo jackpot's pool to its 200.00 limit (where the win chance is 100%), evaluates the reward, and checks the pool reset — then replays the evaluation to prove a winner is not paid twice.

With Kafka, contribution is asynchronous: the pool checks retry themselves a few times while the consumer catches up. Setting a 300 ms delay in the Runner makes that quieter. In `no-kafka` mode the loopback publisher contributes in-process, so the first attempt already sees the new pool.

item.name: Jackpots
item.description: Read the seeded jackpots and what has been contributed to them. H2 is in-memory, so restarting the app restores exactly this state.

request.description:
The three seeded jackpots with their current pool and their contribution/reward configuration:

| Jackpot | Initial pool | Contribution | Reward chance |
|---|---|---|---|
| fixed (`1111...`) | 10 000 | fixed 5% | fixed 10% |
| variable (`2222...`) | 5 000 | 10% → 2%, -1 point per 1 000 of growth | 1% → +2 points per 1 000 of growth, certain at 20 000 |
| demo (`3333...`) | 100 | fixed 10% | 5% → +10 points per 50 of growth, certain at 200 |

Names identify a jackpot to humans, so they are unique. The service rejects the duplicate before writing, and a unique index on the column is the backstop if two creates race past that check.

item.name: Delete it now it has contributions (409)

request.description: Deleting it would orphan the contribution row, so the request is refused.

item.name: Create with an incomplete VARIABLE config (400)

request.description:
`percentage` alone is enough for a FIXED contribution but not for a VARIABLE one. Each shape is its own record and validates itself in its constructor, so an incomplete config is rejected at the boundary rather than being stored as a half-null row.

Note the trade: the record constructor throws on the first missing value, so the response names one field at a time rather than all of them at once.

exec: pm.test("the response names the field that is missing", () => {

item.name: Bets
item.description: Use cases 1-3: publish a bet, which is consumed off the `jackpot-bets` topic and contributed to its matching jackpot.

request.description:
Publishes the bet to the `jackpot-bets` Kafka topic (202 Accepted). The consumer then contributes it to the matching jackpot.

The bet is contributed **and evaluated** by the pipeline; the reward requests below read that outcome. The pre-request script generates a fresh `betId` on every send — contribution is idempotent per bet id, so re-sending the same id is a deliberate no-op (see "Publish the same bet twice").

exec: // A fresh id per send; contribution is idempotent per betId.
pm.test("the accepted bet is echoed back", () => {
" - evaluate it with the reward request, or watch the pool grow.");

request.description: Re-publishes the bet id from the previous request. Kafka may redeliver and clients retry, so a bet contributes at most once — the app logs `already contributed ... skipping` and the pool does not move. Send "Get one jackpot" before and after to see it stay put.

exec: pm.test("202 Accepted (the duplicate is skipped downstream, not rejected)", () => {

item.name: Publish a bet on an unknown jackpot (404)

request.description:
The jackpot is checked before the bet is published, so this is rejected with 404 and nothing reaches the `jackpot-bets` topic.

The alternative — accept it, publish it, and let the consumer skip it — costs a message, a consumer round trip and a log line, and tells the client nothing. The consumer keeps its own "no matching jackpot" branch anyway, because the jackpot could be removed between this check and delivery.
A blank `betId` and a non-positive `betAmount`. Bean Validation rejects the request before anything is published, and the handler returns a `ProblemDetail` listing every field error.

item.name: Reward
item.description: Use case 4. The draw happens once, in the pipeline, immediately after the bet contributes — so these are reads. Asking again always gives the same answer.

request.description:
Reads the outcome decided when the bet was processed. 200 either way — read `won`. The response also carries the chance the draw was made against and the value that came up, so an outcome can be explained rather than taken on trust.

404 means the bet has not been evaluated: it named a jackpot that does not exist, or it has not been consumed off the topic yet.

The same request again. Because every evaluation is persisted — win **or** loss — this is a read of the same row, byte for byte.

When the draw lived in the endpoint and only wins were stored, a loss left no trace and could be retried until it won: with a flat 10% chance, 22 calls gave a 90% chance of taking the pool, at no cost.

exec: pm.test("the response is identical to the first one", () => {

request.description: It is a read. A POST would imply asking for a fresh draw, which is exactly the bug that was fixed.

item.name: A bet that was never evaluated (404)

request.description: Only a bet that contributed to a jackpot is evaluated. This bet id was never accepted (its jackpot does not exist), so there is no outcome to read.

item.name: Walkthrough - win a jackpot
item.description:
An ordered, self-checking run ending in a guaranteed win.

Run it with the Collection Runner. It uses the demo jackpot, whose variable reward chance reaches 100% once the pool hits its 200.00 limit — so the win is arithmetic, not luck.

Note what is **not** here: a request that asks the service to draw. The bet is evaluated by the pipeline the moment it contributes; the last steps only read what was already decided.

item.name: 1. The demo jackpot starts at its initial pool

request.description: Baseline. The demo jackpot starts at 100.00, takes a flat 10% of every stake, and is guaranteed to pay out once its pool reaches 200.00. The test records the current pool so the later steps assert relative to it.

exec: pm.test("it takes a flat 10% of every stake", () => {
pm.test("its reward is guaranteed once the pool reaches 200.00", () => {

item.name: 2. Publish one bet big enough to reach the limit

request.description: 10% of a 1000.00 stake is 100.00 — enough to take the pool from its seeded 100.00 to the 200.00 limit. The bet is then evaluated immediately, by the pipeline, against the pool it just filled. Nothing needs to ask.

item.name: 3. The pipeline already decided the outcome

request.description: No request asked for a draw — the bet was evaluated when it was consumed. Under Kafka that is asynchronous, so this retries until the outcome appears.

exec: pm.test("it was paid the pool it had just filled", () => {

item.name: 4. The pool reset to its initial amount

request.description: An awarded jackpot starts over: the pool goes back to the configured initial amount, and with it the variable curves, which are derived from pool growth.

exec: pm.test("the pool reset to the initial amount", () => {

request.description: The contribution row is the persisted record of the bet: bet id, user id, jackpot id, stake, contribution and the pool at that moment.

item.name: 6. Asking again returns the identical outcome

request.description: The safety property that matters: the outcome is a stored fact, so no amount of asking pays a second time or changes what happened.
